title: Caring for the place we share: litter, plants and small animals

summary.text: A toffee wrapper dropped on the road does not stay there. Rain and wind carry light litter along, into drains, rivers and the mouths of animals. Your child puts clean litter on the bathroom floor, pours a mug of 'rain', and watches where each thing goes. Then we look after the beings who share our home: we water a plant only when the soil is dry, and we carry a small visitor outside gently. Our environment is everything around us, and every living being in it needs it clean.
summary.art: A city lane in the rain: a toffee wrapper floating along the water towards a drain grill, a crow on a wall, a cow by a gate, and a girl on a balcony with a potted tulsi.

intro.hook: Drop a scrap of paper in front of the fan. Where does the paper land?
intro.text: The paper does not stay where you dropped it. The moving air carries it across the room. Rain does the same thing to litter outside. Litter is rubbish left where it does not belong. In this unit we find out where litter goes, and who it meets on the way. Then we learn how to care for the plants and small animals who live near us.
intro.art: A girl dropping a small scrap of paper in front of a table fan, and the paper flying across the room while her little brother points.

outcomes: By the end I can say what our environment is: everything around us, living and not living.
By the end I can say where rain and wind take litter, from my own test.
By the end I can say how litter can hurt cows, birds and drains.
By the end I can put rubbish in the right bin: wet waste or dry waste.
By the end I can tell if a potted plant needs water, with the finger test.
By the end I can move a small animal outside gently, without hurting them.

terms.meaning: Your environment is everything around you. It has living beings, like plants, birds and people, and things that are not alive, like air, water and soil.
terms.example: Your balcony, the tulsi pot on it, the crow on the railing, the air and the rain are all part of your environment.
terms.art: A balcony scene with a tulsi pot, a crow on the railing, rain clouds above and a girl looking out, with gentle arrows pointing to each.

terms.meaning: Litter is rubbish left where it does not belong, like on a road, in a park or by a drain.
terms.example: A chips packet lying on the steps of a building is litter. The same packet inside a bin is not.
terms.art: Two pictures side by side: a chips packet on the steps of a building, and the same packet inside a dustbin.

terms.meaning: A drain is a channel or pipe that carries rainwater and used water away from homes and roads.
terms.example: The hole with a grill on your bathroom floor is a drain. So is the channel along the side of your street.
terms.art: A bathroom floor drain with a steel grill, and beside it a street drain with water running in.

terms.meaning: Wet waste is food and plant rubbish that rots, like peels and leftover rice. Dry waste is rubbish that does not rot quickly, like plastic, paper, glass and metal.
terms.example: A banana peel goes in the wet waste bin. A milk packet goes in the dry waste bin.
terms.art: Two small bins, a green one with a banana peel and tea leaves, and a blue one with a milk packet and a newspaper.

explanations.concept: Our environment is everything around us
explanations.definition: The environment is everything around a living being: the air, water, soil and light, and all the other living beings nearby.
explanations.description: Your environment is your room, your building, your lane and the sky above, not only far-away forests. Plants, crows, ants, cows and people all share it. Humans are animals too, so we need clean air, clean water and a safe place, just like the others.
examples: The air you breathe in your room is part of your environment.
The neem tree by your gate, and the squirrels in the tree, are part of your environment.
The rain that falls on your roof and runs into the drain is part of your environment.
explanations.context: This card says what the word environment means.
explanations.art: A cut-away picture of a city building with a family inside, a neem tree outside with a squirrel, a crow on the roof, rain falling and a drain at the bottom.

explanations.concept: Litter does not stay where it is dropped
explanations.definition: Litter is rubbish left where it does not belong. Rain and wind move light litter from place to place.
explanations.description: A toffee wrapper, a plastic bag or a paper cup is very light. Wind blows light litter along, and rainwater carries it down the road. Most thin plastic floats, so the water can carry it a long way, to a drain, a river or the sea. The person who dropped it never sees where it ends up.
examples: In the Bathroom Rain Test, the wrapper rode the water to the drain, but the pebble stayed.
On a windy day, plastic bags get caught in trees and on wires.
After heavy rain, plastic and wrappers pile up at the mouth of a drain.
explanations.context: This card explains what we saw in the Bathroom Rain Test: where rain and wind take litter.
explanations.art: A wrapper's path drawn as a dotted line: from a hand on a road, along a rainy gutter, into a drain, and out to a river with a fish.

explanations.concept: How litter hurts living beings and drains
explanations.definition: Litter can hurt living beings who eat it or get stuck in it, and it can block drains so that rainwater floods the street.
explanations.description: Cows in Indian towns often eat plastic bags with food scraps inside. The plastic stays in the cow's stomach and can make her very ill. Birds and fish can swallow plastic or get tangled in plastic bags and nets. Litter also piles up on drain grills, so rainwater cannot get away and the street floods.
examples: A cow nosing at a plastic bag of leftover food by a gate.
A street in the monsoon flooded because plastic blocked the drain.
Mosquito eggs in rainwater inside an old paper cup on a terrace. Mosquitoes lay eggs in small pools of still water.
explanations.context: This card explains why litter matters: who it can hurt.
explanations.art: Three small pictures: a cow sniffing a plastic bag, a drain grill covered in wrappers with water pooling above it, and an old cup holding rainwater.

explanations.concept: Plants and small animals near us feel and choose
explanations.description: Plants and animals near us sense what is around them and act on it. A plant in dry soil closes the tiny holes in the leaves to keep water in. An ant who finds sugar leaves a smell trail on the way home, and other ants follow it. Plants and ants feel, remember and decide. Some scientists say these are automatic actions, like a machine. So we care for them gently, as we would want to be cared for.
examples: A tulsi plant's leaves droop on a hot afternoon when the soil is dry, and lift again after watering.
Ants walk in a line along a smell trail to sugar on a counter.
A crow opens her beak and pants on a very hot day to cool down.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who study plants and insects
perspectives.explanation: Plants and ants sense, remember and choose. A plant who meets dry soil keeps water in, and ants choose the shortest way to food. This is their own kind of thinking.
These are automatic responses, built into the body, like a door that opens when you step near it. They say it is better not to call this thinking.

explanations.context: This card is about the plants and small animals who share our home.
explanations.art: A drooping tulsi plant next to a lifted one after watering, a line of ants walking to a few grains of sugar, and a crow with an open beak in the shade.

agreed.text: Rain and wind carry litter from where it is dropped to drains, rivers and the sea.
agreed.evidence: People who clean beaches and rivers find wrappers and bags that came from towns far upstream. In the Bathroom Rain Test, one mug of water carried a wrapper to the drain.

agreed.text: Plastic litter blocks drains and makes floods worse.
agreed.evidence: City workers in India clear piles of plastic from drains before every monsoon. Where drains are blocked, rainwater stays on the streets.

agreed.text: Plastic can hurt animals who eat it or get tangled in it.
agreed.evidence: Vets in India have found plastic bags inside the stomachs of cows who roam the streets. Seabirds, turtles and fish around the world have been found with plastic inside them.

challenging.claim: One small wrapper does no harm.
challenging.for: One wrapper is tiny. On its own, one wrapper will not block a big drain.
challenging.against: Many people each drop one wrapper, and the rain carries them all to the same few drains. Together they block the grill. In the Bathroom Rain Test, even one wrapper stuck on the grill.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that a small piece of litter does not matter.

challenging.claim: A banana peel is fine to throw anywhere, because it rots.
challenging.for: A banana peel does rot, and it does not stay for years like plastic.
challenging.against: A peel takes weeks to rot. On a road, someone can slip on it. In a lane, it brings flies and rats. Peels rot best in a wet waste bin or a compost pot.
challenging.context: This card is about peels and other food waste: can we leave them anywhere?

challenging.claim: Feeding bread to crows and pigeons is always kind.
challenging.for: Birds are hungry, and feeding them can help in a hard season. Many families put out rice for crows.
challenging.against: Bread fills birds up without giving them what their bodies need. Food left in piles brings rats, and very large flocks of pigeons can make people ill with their droppings. Clean water in a shallow plate on a hot day helps birds without these problems.
challenging.context: This card is about feeding the birds near our home: does it always help them?

big_questions.q: Why does a wrapper ride on water, but a pebble stays on the floor?
big_questions.hint: Think about which one is lighter, and which one floats.

big_questions.q: How does a plant know that the soil is dry?
big_questions.hint: Think about the roots in the soil. What do they touch?

big_questions.q: When we say 'our lane', whose lane is it: ours, the crow's, the cow's or the ant's?
big_questions.hint: Who lives there? Who uses the lane every day? Was anyone there before the houses?

big_questions.q: If nobody ever saw where their litter went, would they still care?
big_questions.hint: Think about the wrapper in the drain. Who saw it there?

story.title: The Red Wrapper
story.note: Nila, Arun, Ammamma and Selvi akka are made up. What the rain, the wrappers, the drain and the cow do in the story really happens in Indian towns.
text: Nila lived on the second floor of a yellow building in Chennai. She was seven. Her little brother Arun was five. Their grandmother, Ammamma, lived with them and grew tulsi and jasmine on the balcony.
One Monday afternoon, Arun ate a toffee on the balcony. He held the red wrapper up high. A gust of wind snatched it out of his fingers. The wrapper floated over the railing and down into the lane.
"Arun, your wrapper!" said Nila.
"It's only a tiny one," said Arun. "Nobody will notice."
On Thursday, the big rain came. The northeast monsoon rain fell all night. In the morning, the lane was a brown river. The water came right up to the first step of their building.
"The drain at the corner must be blocked again," said Ammamma. "Look how the water stays."

When the rain stopped, Ammamma, Nila and Arun went down with an umbrella. At the corner, a woman in a green coat was working at the drain with a long rake. Her name was Selvi akka, and she cleaned the drains on their street.

The drain grill was covered with a thick mat of litter. There were chips packets, plastic bags, paper cups and wrappers, all pressed flat by the water. Selvi akka pulled the mat away with her rake. With a loud gurgle, the water rushed into the drain. Slowly, the lane came back.
Nila looked at the pile. Right on top lay a red toffee wrapper.
"Arun! That could be yours," she said.
"It can't be," said Arun. "Mine fell outside our gate. That's far away."
Selvi akka laughed kindly. "Every wrapper on this street comes here in the end," she said. "The rain brings them all to my drain."
Next to the gate, a brown cow was sniffing a plastic bag with old rice inside. Ammamma gently pulled the bag away and put the rice on a banana leaf for her. She dropped the bag in the dry waste bin.
"Cows can't tell the plastic from the food," said Ammamma. "The plastic stays inside them and makes them ill."
At home, Nila had an idea. She took Arun into the bathroom. She put a clean wrapper and a pebble on the floor, a little way from the drain. "This is our lane," she said. "Now watch the rain."
She poured a mug of water on the floor. The pebble stayed where it was. But the wrapper floated, turned round once, and slid all the way to the drain. There it stuck flat on the grill.
Arun stared. "The rain took it for a ride," he said slowly. "My wrapper went to Selvi akka's drain."
"Maybe that one, maybe another one," said Nila. "But it could have been yours."
That evening, Arun made a pocket from an old envelope. He wrote BIN on it in big crooked letters. Every wrapper went in his pocket bin until he got home.

On the balcony, Ammamma's tulsi was drooping after the hot afternoon. Arun pushed his finger into the soil, the way Ammamma had shown him. The soil was dry. He gave the tulsi a little water. By night, the leaves had lifted up again.
"Now the tulsi is happy, and the drain is happy," said Arun.
"And the cow," said Nila.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Arun thinks a small wrapper stays where it falls and harms nobody. Nila shows him with a mug of water that rain carries light litter along the ground until it reaches a drain, where it piles up with everyone else's and blocks the water. What one person drops travels to places, and beings, they never see.
ask: Where did the wind take Arun's wrapper on Monday?
Why did the lane fill with water on Thursday?
What did Nila show Arun in the bathroom? What happened to the pebble, and to the wrapper?
How did Arun know the tulsi needed water?
art: A small boy on a city balcony holding up a red toffee wrapper while the wind lifts it away, his sister and grandmother watching.
A lane flooded with brown rainwater up to the first step of a yellow building.
A woman in a green coat clearing a mat of wrappers and plastic bags from a drain grill with a long rake, while water rushes in.
A grandmother putting rice on a banana leaf for a brown cow, holding a plastic bag in her other hand.

games.title: Fly, Float or Stay: a moving game about litter
games.context: This is a moving game about where litter goes. The grown-up holds up a card and calls 'Wind!' or 'Rain!'. You act out what that piece of litter would do: fly, float or stay still.

printables.title: 10 litter cards to cut out, with what wind and rain do on the back

items.b: Wind: flies far. Rain: floats away to the drain.
Wind: flies and catches on trees. Rain: floats far.
Wind: tumbles along the ground. Rain: floats a little way, then goes soggy and stays.
Wind: flies far. Rain: floats away to the drain.
Wind: flies. Rain: floats a little way.
Wind: flies. Rain: goes soggy and sticks down, so it stays.
Wind: stays. Rain: stays, or slides a tiny bit.

rules: Clear a space on the floor to move in. Choose one wall to be the drain.
The grown-up mixes the cards, picks one and reads the front aloud.
If the thing would fly or tumble in the wind, run round the room on tiptoe with your arms out.
If the thing would float far on rain, sway and slide slowly to the drain wall. If it floats only a little way, slide a few steps and freeze.
If the thing would stay, freeze like a statue.
The grown-up reads the back of the card. Did you move the right way? Then pick the next card.
When all 10 cards have been used, the game is over. Everyone who moved the right way on most cards is a winner, so two players, or four, can all win.

setup.art: A grown-up holding up a card that says 'Toffee wrapper' and calling 'Wind!', with two children in a cleared room.
setup.caption: 1. Pick a card and call 'Wind!' or 'Rain!'.

setup.art: One child running on tiptoe with arms out like a flying wrapper, another frozen like a pebble.
setup.caption: 2. Fly, float or freeze.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 10 cards. 2. Read the front of each card aloud. 3. Clear a space and choose one wall to be the drain.
flow.say: Each card is a piece of litter. When I call 'Wind!' or 'Rain!', show me what that litter would do.
flow.kid: Each card is litter. Listen for 'Wind!' or 'Rain!'. Then fly, float or freeze.

flow.do: Pick a card, read the front, and call 'Wind!' or 'Rain!'. Watch what your child does. Then read the back aloud.
flow.say: Toffee wrapper. Wind! Show me. Why did you fly?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Is it light or heavy? Fly, float or freeze.

ask.q: Why does the wrapper fly, but the pebble stays?
good: The pebble is too heavy for the wind.
The wind can lift light things.

flow.parent: If your child has done the Bathroom Rain Test, ask what they saw there. The answers on the backs come from that kind of test.

flow.do: Lay all the cards out in two rows: the ones that fly or float, and the ones that stay.
flow.say: Look at the two rows. Which row should never be dropped outside? Why?
flow.kid: Make two rows: fly or float, and stay. Which row travels far?

check.q: Which litter will the rain carry furthest?
check.why: A plastic bag is light and floats, so rainwater carries the bag a long way. A pebble and a spoon are heavy and stay where they are.

games.title: Helping Pairs: a memory game about caring for our neighbours
games.context: This is a memory game. Half the cards show a neighbour who needs help: a plant, an animal or a drain. The other half show a kind thing to do. Find a neighbour and the help that fits.

printables.title: 12 cards to cut out: 6 neighbours and 6 kind acts
items: Water slowly at the roots, until the soil is damp
Wipe up the crumbs, and carry the ant out on a paper
Crow panting on a hot ledge
A shallow plate of water in the shade
Switch off the light and open the window

img.credit: Swarochi Tathagath, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items: Walk round her, and do not pick her up
Pick it up and put it in the dry waste bin

rules: Mix the 12 cards and lay them face down in rows.
Take turns. Turn over two cards. The grown-up reads them aloud.
If you find a neighbour and the help that fits, say why it helps. Keep both cards.
If they do not fit, turn them face down again in the same places.
When all the cards are taken, the game is over. Count your pairs. The most pairs wins, and players with the same number share the win. If you play as a team, the goal is to find all 6 pairs.

setup.art: Twelve cards face down on a mat in three rows, with a girl and a grown-up sitting beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the 12 cards face down.

setup.art: A girl turning over two cards: 'Crow panting on a hot ledge' and 'A shallow plate of water in the shade'.
setup.caption: 2. Find a neighbour and the help that fits.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. 2. Read each one aloud once, so your child hears them. 3. Mix them and lay them face down in rows.
flow.say: Some cards show a neighbour who needs help. Some show a kind thing to do. Let's match them.
flow.kid: Some cards show who needs help. Some show what helps. Find the pairs.

flow.do: Take turns turning over two cards. When a pair fits, ask your child why.
flow.say: You found the crow and the plate of water. Why does a shallow plate in the shade help the crow?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Do they fit? Say why.

ask.q: Why do we carry the ant outside, instead of squashing the ant?
good: The ant was only looking for food.

ask.q: Why should the bird's water be shallow?
good: So small birds can stand in it.
So they do not fall in and drown.

flow.parent: Accept any pair your child can explain well. For the snail, the kind act is to leave her where she is. Snails can carry germs, so wash hands if anyone touches one.

flow.do: Count the pairs. Then choose one kind act to do for real today.
flow.say: Which kind act can we do today, here at home?
flow.kid: Count your pairs. Pick one kind act to do today.

check.q: A money plant's soil is dry. What helps?
options: Put the plant in a dark cupboard
check.why: Dry soil means the roots have no water to drink. Watering slowly at the roots lets the water soak in.

experiments.title: The Bathroom Rain Test: where does water carry litter?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put five clean bits of litter on the bathroom floor, a little way from the drain. You pour a mug of water to be the rain, and watch where each one goes. Then you try the wind, with a fan.
experiments.question: When rain falls, does litter stay where it was dropped, or does the water carry it away? Which kinds go furthest?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which of the five things will the water carry to the drain? Which will stay where they are? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All five things start in one row, the same distance from the drain. We pour the same mug of water from the same place each time. Only the things are different.
results_table: Did the water carry it to the drain?
Did the fan blow it away?

materials.item: a bathroom floor with a drain, or a big steel plate tilted on a book over a bucket
water in a mug, filled again for each pour
a clean toffee wrapper or chips packet
a piece of a thin plastic bag, about as big as your palm
two scraps of newspaper, each about as big as your palm (keep one dry for the fan)
a piece of banana peel or any vegetable peel
a pebble, or a steel spoon
a table fan, or a newspaper folded into a hand fan

experiments.safety: A wet bathroom floor is slippery. Walk slowly, and wipe the floor dry at the end. A grown-up switches the fan on and off, and fingers stay away from the blades.

schedule.what: Guess, pour the rain three times, try the fan, then sort the litter into the right bins.

experiments.record: Draw the bathroom floor and the drain. Draw an arrow for each thing that moved, showing where it went. Draw a circle round each thing that stayed.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from one family in Kochi
rows: A little, then it stuck down wet

setup.art: Five clean things in a row on a bathroom floor about half a big step from the drain: a wrapper, a bit of plastic bag, a newspaper scrap, a banana peel and a pebble.
setup.caption: 1. Put five things in a row, half a step from the drain.

setup.art: A child pouring a mug of water onto the floor just behind the row, with the water spreading towards the drain.
setup.caption: 2. Pour a mug of water behind the row: the rain.

setup.art: The wrapper and the plastic piece stuck flat on the drain grill, with a little water pooling around them, while the pebble stays in place.
setup.caption: 3. Look: what went to the drain, and what stayed?

setup.art: A table fan blowing across a dry floor, with the wrapper and the newspaper flying off and the pebble and peel staying.
setup.caption: 4. Now try the wind, with a fan on a dry floor.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the five things. 2. Let them hold each one. 3. Lay them in a row, half a big step from the drain. 4. Choose the side where water runs to the drain.
flow.say: These five things are litter on a road. This hole is the drain. Hold each one. Which feel light? Which feel heavy?
flow.kid: Hold each thing. Which is light? Which is heavy? Put them in a row.
flow.parent: Use only clean litter. Choose the side of the floor that slopes towards the drain. If your bathroom has no drain, tilt a big steel plate on a book over a bucket, and put the things on the plate.

flow.do: Ask for a guess for each thing, and the reason. The grown-up writes the guesses in the table.
flow.say: When I pour the rain, which things will the water carry to the drain? Which will stay? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess: which will go to the drain? Which will stay? Why?

ask.q: Which do you think will reach the drain? Why?
good: The wrapper, because it is light.
Not the pebble, because it is heavy.

flow.parent: Wait for a guess and a reason for each thing before you pour. Do not say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Pour one mug of water slowly onto the floor, just behind the row. 2. Watch together. 3. The grown-up marks in the table what moved. 4. Put the things back in the row and pour again. Do it three times.
flow.say: Here comes the rain. Watch each one. Where did the wrapper go? Where did the pebble go? Let's pour two more times, because one try can be a fluke.
flow.kid: Watch the rain. What moved? What stayed? Try three times.

good: The wrapper got stuck on the grill.
The water had to go round it.

flow.parent: Usually the wrapper and the plastic float and ride the water to the drain, and stick flat on the grill. The newspaper gets soggy and sticks to the floor. The peel may slide a little. The pebble stays. If nothing reaches the drain, move the row closer and pour from a little higher.

flow.do: 1. Pick up the wet things and dry them on a cloth. Put the wet newspaper aside and use the dry one. 2. Move to a dry floor in another room. 3. Lay the five things in a row. 4. The grown-up switches the fan on low, about one big step away, or fans hard with folded newspaper.
flow.say: Now the wind. Which things will the fan blow away? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Now the wind. Guess first. Then watch the fan blow.

ask.q: Which things did the wind blow away?

flow.parent: The light, dry things fly: the wrapper, the plastic and the dry newspaper. The peel and the pebble stay. A weak fan may not move the heavier wrapper: move the row closer.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they saw, and why. Then look back at their guesses.
flow.say: Tell me what happened, and why. Was your guess right? If a wrapper is dropped on our road, where could the rain take it?
flow.kid: Say what you saw. Was your guess right? Where would the rain take a wrapper on our road?

ask.q: Where could a wrapper on our road end up?
good: In the river or the sea.
Blocking the drain, so the road floods.

check.q: In our test, which stayed where it was put?
check.why: The pebble is heavy, so the water flowed round it. The wrapper and the plastic are light and float, so the water carried them away.

flow.do: 1. Put the wrapper, plastic and newspaper in the dry waste bin. 2. Put the peel in the wet waste bin. 3. Wipe the bathroom floor dry. 4. Wash hands.
flow.say: Litter goes in a bin, where the rain cannot carry it. Which bin does the peel go in? Which bin for the wrapper?
flow.kid: Put each thing in the right bin. The peel is wet waste. The wrapper is dry waste.

experiments.title: The Sugar Test: do ants find food left out?
experiments.context: In this experiment you leave a few grains of sugar where you have seen ants. You come back after half an hour to see who has found them. Then you wipe across the ants' path with a soapy cloth and watch what the ants do.
experiments.question: If we leave a few grains of sugar out, will ants find them? If we wipe across their path, what will the ants do?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will any ants come to the sugar in half an hour? If we wipe across their path, will they keep walking, or stop? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We put the same pinch of sugar in the same place, and look after the same time. For the wipe, we wipe only one strip across the path, and leave the rest of the path alone.
results_table: How many ants? (none, a few, many)
Walking in a line, or all over?
What did they do at the wiped strip?

materials.item: a pinch of sugar on a small square of paper
a place where you have seen ants, such as the edge of the kitchen counter or a window ledge
a cloth dipped in soapy water and squeezed out
a clock or a phone timer

schedule.what: Put the sugar paper down where ants come. Guess, and note the time.
Half an hour later: look, count and watch the ants. Wipe one strip across their path and watch for five minutes.
Carry the sugar paper outside for the ants, and wipe the counter clean.

experiments.record: Draw the sugar paper and the ants. Draw their path as a dotted line. Draw the wiped strip, and what the ants did there.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from one family in Guwahati
rows: In a line from a crack to the sugar
They stopped, waved their feelers and wandered, then found the path again

setup.art: A small square of paper with a pinch of sugar on it, at the edge of a kitchen counter near a crack in the tiles.
setup.caption: 1. Leave a pinch of sugar where ants come.

setup.art: A line of small ants walking from a crack in the tiles to the sugar paper.
setup.caption: 2. After half an hour, look. Who came?

setup.art: A hand wiping one strip across the line of ants with a cloth, and ants on both sides stopping and turning.
setup.caption: 3. Wipe one strip across their path. Watch.

flow.do: 1. Put the sugar paper down where you have seen ants. 2. Note the time. 3. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: We are leaving a little food out, like a crumb after a snack. Will anyone find the sugar? How long will they take? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put the sugar down. Who will find the sugar? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Who might come to the sugar?
good: Nobody, because there is no smell.

flow.parent: Choose a place where you have seen ants before. Most Indian homes have them somewhere.

flow.do: Leave the sugar for half an hour.
flow.say: Now we wait. The ants have to find the sugar by themselves.
flow.kid: Now we wait for half an hour.
flow.wait: Leave the sugar for about half an hour.
flow.parent: If no ants come in half an hour, look again after two hours. If none come at all, try a window ledge or the balcony on another day. You can still talk about why food left out brings ants.

flow.do: Look closely together. Count roughly: none, a few or many. Look for a line of ants coming and going.
flow.say: Who found the sugar? Are the ants walking anywhere, or in a line? Where does the line come from?
flow.kid: Look closely. Are there ants? Are they in a line? Where does the line start?

ask.q: Why do the ants walk in a line?
good: They are going home with the sugar.

flow.parent: An ant who finds food leaves a smell trail on the way home. Other ants follow the smell to the food, and add their own smell. That is why they walk in a line.

flow.do: Wipe one strip across the ants' path with the soapy cloth, a hand's width away from the sugar. Do not wipe the ants themselves. Watch for five minutes.
flow.say: I am wiping away a strip of the path. What will the ants do when they reach the wiped part? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Watch the ants at the wiped strip. What do they do?

ask.q: What did the ants do at the wiped strip?
good: They waved their feelers and walked all over.

flow.parent: The soap wipes away the smell trail. The ants usually stop, wave their feelers, called antennae, and wander about until they find the smell again. Ants do not always stop: if they walk straight across, wipe the strip again, a little wider. This shows the path is a smell, not a road they can see.

check.q: How do ants find the way to the sugar?
options: They follow a smell trail left by other ants
They read the signs on the wall
check.why: An ant who finds food leaves a smell trail. Other ants follow that smell. When we wiped the strip, the smell was gone, so the ants were lost for a while.

flow.do: 1. Carry the sugar paper out to the balcony or a window ledge. 2. Wipe the counter where the sugar was. 3. Ask the last question.
flow.say: The ants were only looking for food. Let's give them the sugar outside. Why do ants come into homes? How can we keep them outside?
flow.kid: Carry the sugar outside for the ants. How can we keep ants out of the kitchen?

ask.q: How can we stop ants coming into the kitchen?

activities.title: Clean Corner: make one place better
activities.context: In this activity you find one place in your home or building that needs care. You draw it, make it better, and draw it again.

materials.item: paper and crayons
the wet waste and dry waste bins
a broom and a dustpan, or a dry cloth

activities.safety: Never pick up broken glass, blades, needles or dirty tissues with your hands. Call a grown-up, who uses gloves, tongs or a dustpan.

schedule.what: Choose a corner, draw it, clean it, draw it again.

activities.record: Two drawings side by side: the corner before, and the corner after.

setup.art: A corner of a building's staircase landing with a chips packet, dry leaves and dust, and a child drawing it on paper.
setup.caption: 1. Find a corner that needs care, and draw it.

setup.art: The same child sweeping the leaves into a dustpan and dropping the packet in a blue dry waste bin.
setup.caption: 2. Clean it, and put each thing in the right bin.

setup.art: The clean corner, and two drawings side by side: before and after.
setup.caption: 3. Draw it again. What changed?

flow.do: Walk around your home, balcony or staircase together. Let your child choose one small corner that needs care.
flow.say: Let's find one place near us that needs looking after. Which corner looks sad?
flow.kid: Find one corner that needs care. Choose it.

flow.do: Your child draws the corner as it is now.
flow.say: Draw the corner just as it is now.
flow.kid: Draw the corner now.

flow.do: Clean the corner together. Sort each thing: wet waste, dry waste, or keep.
flow.say: Is this peel wet waste or dry waste? What about this wrapper?
flow.kid: Clean the corner. Put each thing in the right bin.

ask.q: Why does the peel go in a different bin from the wrapper?
good: The wrapper is plastic and does not rot.
So they can be made into new things or into soil.

flow.parent: Do the sharp, broken or dirty things yourself, with gloves or tongs.

flow.do: Your child draws the corner again, next to the first drawing.
flow.say: Draw it again. What is different? Who might like this corner better now?
flow.kid: Draw the corner again. Who will like this corner now?

ask.q: Who might like this corner better now?
good: The ants, because there are no crumbs to fight over.
The plant, because there is room now.

activities.title: The Finger Test: does our plant need water? (if you have a potted plant)
activities.context: In this activity you check if a potted plant needs water, using your finger. A plant who gets too little water droops. A plant who gets too much water can get rotten roots. So we water only when the soil is dry.

materials.item: a potted plant, such as tulsi, a money plant or a chilli plant
a small mug or a bottle of water

schedule.what: Do the finger test. Water only if the soil is dry. Look again in the evening.

activities.record: Draw your plant. Draw a finger in the soil, and write 'dry' or 'damp'.

setup.art: A child's finger pushed into the soil of a tulsi pot, up to the first bend of the finger.
setup.caption: 1. Push your finger into the soil, up to the first bend.

setup.art: A child pouring a little water slowly at the base of the tulsi, near the stem, with a drop coming out of the pot's hole below.
setup.caption: 2. Dry? Water slowly at the roots. Damp? Wait.

flow.do: 1. Look at the plant's leaves together. 2. Your child pushes one finger into the soil, up to the first bend.
flow.say: Look at the leaves. Are they standing up or drooping? Now feel the soil with your finger. Is it dry or damp?
flow.kid: Look at the leaves. Push your finger into the soil. Dry or damp?

ask.q: Is the soil dry or damp? How can you tell?
good: Damp, my finger is cool and has soil stuck on it.

flow.parent: The first bend of a child's finger is about 2 centimetres deep. The top of the soil can look dry when the soil below is still damp, so we feel below the top.

flow.do: If the soil is dry, your child pours water slowly near the stem. Stop when a little comes out of the bottom hole. If the soil is damp, do not water.
flow.say: If the soil is dry, the roots have nothing to drink. Pour slowly, near the stem. Stop when water comes out of the hole at the bottom.
flow.kid: Dry soil? Pour water slowly near the stem. Damp soil? Wait.
flow.parent: Too much water fills the soil and the roots cannot breathe. That is why we check first. Stand the pot on a tray or in the sink while you water.

flow.do: Look at the plant again in the evening.
flow.say: This evening, let's look at the leaves again. What do you think we will see?
flow.kid: Look at the leaves again this evening. Did they change?
flow.think: Where does the extra water go when it runs out of the hole at the bottom?

activities.title: Kind Hands: moving a small visitor outside
activities.context: In this activity you move a small animal, like an ant, a moth or a beetle, out of the house gently, using a cup and a piece of card. Do it when a small visitor comes in, or with an ant on the balcony.

materials.item: a clear cup or a small glass
a postcard or a piece of stiff paper

activities.safety: Use this only for ants, moths, beetles and grasshoppers. Never try it with bees, wasps, scorpions, centipedes or spiders. Call a grown-up for those. Never touch the visitor with bare hands: a few small beetles can irritate or blister skin.

schedule.what: When a small visitor comes in, move them outside with a cup and a card.

activities.record: Draw your visitor. Write or say where you took them.

setup.art: A clear cup placed gently over a beetle on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Put a cup over the visitor, gently.

setup.art: A postcard slid slowly under the cup, with the beetle walking onto the card.
setup.caption: 2. Slide a card under the cup, slowly.

setup.art: A child lifting the cup on a balcony, next to a potted plant, while the beetle walks away.
setup.caption: 3. Carry them outside. Lift the cup near a plant.

flow.do: Look at the visitor together, without touching. Name them if you can.
flow.say: Look, we have a visitor. Who is this? How many legs? Why might they have come in?
flow.kid: Look at the visitor. Do not touch. Who is this? How many legs?

ask.q: Why might they have come in?

flow.parent: If no visitor comes, use the ants from the Sugar Test.

flow.do: 1. Put the cup over the visitor gently. 2. Slide the card under the cup very slowly. 3. Hold the card against the cup.
flow.say: We move slowly so we do not hurt any legs. Gently now.
flow.kid: Put the cup over them gently. Slide the card under slowly.
flow.parent: Help with the card so no legs get caught. If the visitor is a spider or anything that can sting, move them yourself, or leave a window open for them.

flow.do: Carry the cup to the balcony or a window ledge. Put it down near a plant and lift the cup.
flow.say: Where would a beetle like to be? Let's put them near the plant. Watch where they go.
flow.kid: Carry them outside. Put them near a plant. Lift the cup. Watch.

ask.q: Where did the visitor go when you lifted the cup?

activities.title: Bag in Hand: a trip to the shop with a cloth bag
activities.context: In this activity you take a cloth bag when you go to buy vegetables or groceries. You count how many plastic bags you did not need to take.

materials.item: a cloth bag, or a bag made from an old saree, dupatta or T-shirt
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Go to the shop with a cloth bag. Count the plastic bags you said no to.

activities.record: A tally: one line for each plastic bag you did not take.

setup.art: A girl holding a cloth bag at a vegetable cart while the seller puts tomatoes and beans straight into the bag.
setup.caption: 1. Take a cloth bag to the shop.

setup.art: A paper with tally marks, one for each plastic bag not taken.
setup.caption: 2. Make a tally mark for each plastic bag you did not take.

flow.do: Before you go, your child chooses and carries the cloth bag.
flow.say: Today you are in charge of the bag. When the shop offers a plastic bag, you can say 'No thank you, we have a bag'.
flow.kid: You carry the cloth bag. Say 'No thank you, we have a bag'.

flow.do: At the shop, your child says no to plastic bags and keeps a tally.
flow.say: Every time we say no to a plastic bag, make a line on your paper.
flow.kid: Say no to plastic bags. Make one line each time.

flow.do: At home, count the lines together.
flow.say: How many plastic bags did we not take today? Where could those bags have ended up?
flow.kid: Count your lines. Where could those bags have gone?

ask.q: Where could those plastic bags have ended up?
good: In the dustbin, then in a big rubbish heap.

projects.title: The Pocket Bin: a week of keeping our litter with us
projects.context: In this week-long project you make a small pocket bin from an old envelope or a paper bag. You carry it whenever you go out. Every wrapper or ticket goes into the pocket bin until you reach a dustbin.

materials.item: an old envelope or a small paper bag
crayons or sketch pens
a sheet of paper for a tally

schedule.what: Make and decorate the pocket bin.
Carry the pocket bin when you go out. Make a tally mark for each thing you put in.
Count the whole week's tally. Talk about where those things would have gone.

projects.record: A tally chart for the week, with a small drawing of each kind of thing you kept with you.

setup.art: A boy writing BIN in big letters on an old envelope and drawing a crow on the envelope.
setup.caption: 1. Make a pocket bin from an old envelope.

setup.art: The boy putting a toffee wrapper into the envelope at a bus stop.
setup.caption: 2. When you go out, litter goes in the pocket bin.

setup.art: The boy emptying the envelope into a blue dry waste bin at home, beside a tally sheet.
setup.caption: 3. At home, empty it into the right bin.

flow.do: Your child decorates an old envelope or paper bag and writes BIN on it.
flow.say: This is your pocket bin. When there is no dustbin nearby, the litter waits in here.
flow.kid: Make your pocket bin. Write BIN on it. Draw on it.

flow.do: Each day you go out, your child carries the pocket bin and makes a tally mark for each thing put in. When you get home, empty the pocket bin into the right bin. On day 4, count the marks so far.
flow.say: Where is your pocket bin? Let's make a mark for that wrapper.
flow.kid: Put your litter in the pocket bin. Make a mark each time.
flow.wait: Carry the pocket bin every time you go out this week.

flow.do: On day 7, count all the tally marks together.
flow.say: How many things did you keep with you this week? If each one had been dropped, where could the rain have taken them?
flow.kid: Count all your marks. Where would the rain take those things?

ask.q: If every child in your building made a pocket bin, what would change?
good: The cows would find less plastic.

challenges.title: Beat the Fan: a bin that keeps its litter in
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the Bathroom Rain Test, light litter blew away in the fan's wind. On a windy balcony or by a gate, an open bin can lose its litter the same way. You design a bin that keeps light litter in, even in the wind.
challenges.problem: Make a small bin from things at home that keeps a wrapper and a plastic bit inside when the fan blows on it.
constraints: It must be easy to put litter in.
The fan, on low, one big step away, must not blow the litter out.
It must use things from home, like a box, a tin, a bottle or a bag.
materials: an old box, tin, bucket or a cut plastic bottle
a lid, a piece of cardboard or a cloth
clothes pegs, string or a stone
a wrapper and a piece of plastic bag
a table fan or a folded newspaper fan
general: Put a lid on the bin.
Put a stone on the lid so the wind cannot lift it.
creative: Make a lid with a small slot, so a hand can push litter in but the wind cannot get in.
Use a tall, narrow bin, so the wind blows over the top.
Put the bin in a corner, out of the wind.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your bin. Test it in front of the fan. Did the litter stay in? What would you change?

setup.art: A cardboard box with a lid that has a small slot cut in it, and a stone on top.
setup.caption: 1. Make a bin with a lid.

setup.art: A table fan blowing at the box while a wrapper stays inside and a child watches.
setup.caption: 2. Test it in front of the fan.

flow.do: Remind your child of the fan part of the Bathroom Rain Test. Put a wrapper in an open bowl in front of the fan and switch it on low.
flow.say: Watch the wrapper in the open bowl. What happens? How could we stop the wind taking it?
flow.kid: Watch the open bowl in the wind. How could we keep the wrapper in?
flow.parent: Use a shallow dish or a flat plate, so the wrapper can blow out. If the fan on low does not move it, bring the fan a little closer.

flow.do: Your child chooses materials and builds a bin. A grown-up does the cutting.
flow.say: What will stop the wind? A lid? A heavy stone? A narrow top?
flow.kid: Build your bin. How will it stop the wind?
flow.parent: Cut the opening for your child, and smooth any sharp edge with tape.

flow.do: Put the wrapper and the plastic bit in the bin. Switch the fan on low, one big step away, for a slow count of twenty.
flow.say: Let's test. Did anything blow out? What could make it better?
flow.kid: Test your bin in the wind. Did the litter stay in?

ask.q: What made your bin work, or not work?
good: The lid kept the wind out.
The stone held the lid down.
The wrapper blew out of the gap.

challenges.safety: A grown-up does the cutting: plastic bottles and tins have sharp edges. A grown-up also switches the fan on and off, and fingers stay away from the blades.

quiz.p: Which of these is part of your environment?
quiz.why: The environment is everything around you, living and not living. The air in your room is around you. A dream and a number are inside your mind.

quiz.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 1, drops a toffee wrapper on the road. Then it rains hard. Where will the wrapper most likely go?
opts: It stays in the same place
The rainwater carries the wrapper to a drain
quiz.why: A wrapper is light and floats, so rainwater carries the wrapper along the road to a drain. In our Bathroom Rain Test, the wrapper went to the drain.

quiz.p: Zoya, a girl in Class 1, puts a dry scrap of newspaper and a soaking wet scrap on the floor in front of a fan. Which one flies?
quiz.why: Dry paper is light, so the wind lifts it. Wet paper soaks up water, gets heavy and sticks to the floor.

quiz.p: Why are plastic bags on the street dangerous for cows?
opts: Cows eat the bags with the food inside, and the plastic stays in their stomach
Cows are scared of the colour
quiz.why: Cows cannot sort plastic from food. The plastic does not break down inside them, so it builds up and makes them ill.

quiz.p: After a heavy rain, a street is flooded. What is the most likely reason?
quiz.why: Litter carried by the rain piles up on the drain grill. Then the water cannot get away, so it stays on the street.

quiz.p: Which bin does a banana peel go in?
opts: Neither, throw it on the road
quiz.why: A banana peel is food waste that rots, so it is wet waste. Wet waste can become compost, which feeds plants.

quiz.p: Which bin does an empty milk packet go in?
quiz.why: A milk packet is plastic. Plastic does not rot, so it is dry waste. Rinse the packet first, and it can be recycled.

quiz.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 1, wants to know if his chilli plant needs water. What should he do first?
opts: Push a finger into the soil to feel if it is dry
quiz.why: The finger test tells you what the roots feel. If the soil is dry, water. If the soil is damp, wait, because too much water hurts the roots.

quiz.p: A beetle has walked into the kitchen. What is the kind way to help the beetle?
opts: Put a cup over the beetle, slide a card under, and carry the beetle outside
quiz.why: The cup and card let you carry the beetle out without hurting any legs. The beetle can then find a better place outside.

quiz.p: Ants are walking in a line to a spill of sugar. Why are they in a line?
opts: They follow a smell trail left by the first ant
Someone painted a line for them
quiz.why: An ant who finds food leaves a smell trail on the way home. Other ants follow the smell, so they walk in a line.

items.p: Draw the bathroom floor from your rain test. Draw an arrow to show where the wrapper went. Draw a circle round the thing that stayed.
items.a: An arrow from the wrapper to the drain, and a circle round the pebble.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the light, floating litter going to the drain and the heavy pebble staying, as the child saw.
items.art: An empty square for the bathroom floor, with a small drain drawn in one corner.

items.p: Colour the things the rain will carry away in blue. Colour the things that will stay in brown.
items.why: Light things ride on rainwater. Heavy things stay where they are.
items.art: Six small pictures: a toffee wrapper, a pebble, a plastic bag, a steel spoon, a chips packet and a brick.

items.p: Draw a line from each neighbour to the help they need.
pairs: A little water at the roots
A crow on a hot day
A shallow plate of water in the shade
Carry the ant out on a paper
A drain with a wrapper on top
Put the wrapper in the bin
items.why: Each neighbour needs something different. Looking closely tells us what will help.
items.art: A drooping plant, a crow, an ant and a drain grill on one side, and a mug, a plate, a paper and a bin on the other.

items.p: A wrapper dropped on the road stays in the same place for ever.
items.why: False. Wind and rain carry light litter away, to drains, rivers and the sea. The wrapper moves, but the wrapper does not disappear.

items.p: This is a picture of a lane. Write or say the names: drain, litter, tree, cow.
a: drain: the grill at the side of the road
litter: the wrappers by the gate
tree: the neem by the wall
items.why: Naming the parts helps the child see the whole environment: things that are alive, and things that are not.
items.art: A lane with a neem tree, a cow by a gate, wrappers on the ground and a drain grill at the side of the road.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: why should we put a wrapper in a bin, and not on the road?
items.a: On the road, the rain can carry the wrapper to a drain and block it, or a cow can eat the wrapper. In the bin, it stays put.
items.why: A strong answer says where the wrapper would go, using what the rain test showed, and who it could hurt.

items.p: Two friends in Mysuru see a chips packet in the park.

views.says: It's not mine. The person who dropped it should pick it up.
If we leave the chips packet, the rain will take it to the drain. Let's put it in the bin.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, for example that the rain will carry the packet away and nobody else may pick it up. It also sees that Divya has a point: the person who dropped it did something unfair.
items.why: Both friends are right about something. It is fair that people clear up their own litter. But the packet will still travel, whoever dropped it.

items.p: Count the pieces of litter on this drain grill: 2 wrappers, 1 plastic bag and 3 paper cups.
items.why: 2 and 1 and 3 make 6. Six pieces on one grill can stop the water getting in.
items.art: A drain grill with 2 wrappers, 1 plastic bag and 3 paper cups lying on it.

items.p: A brown cow is nosing at a plastic bag with old rice inside. What should a grown-up do?
opts: Gently take the bag away and put the rice on a leaf
Leave the bag for the cow
items.why: The cow cannot tell the plastic from the rice, and the plastic would stay inside her. Taking the bag away and giving the rice on a leaf feeds her without the plastic.

items.p: You go to buy vegetables. What can you take, so you do not need a plastic bag?
items.why: A cloth bag can go to the shop again and again. A plastic bag is used once, and then it can blow into a drain.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 1, puts a plastic bag piece and a pebble on a steel plate, then tilts the plate and pours water. What will most likely happen?
opts: The plastic slides down, the pebble stays
The pebble slides down, the plastic stays
items.why: Plastic is light and floats on the water, so the water carries the plastic. The pebble is heavy and does not float, so the pebble stays.

items.p: Put the rain test in order.
items: Pour a mug of water behind the row
Put the things in a row near the drain
a: Put the things in a row near the drain
Pour a mug of water behind the row
items.why: First set up, then guess, then test, then look. The guess comes before the test, so the test can show if the guess was right.

items.p: Draw the journey of a toffee wrapper dropped on your road: from a hand, along the road in the rain, to where it ends up.
items.a: A drawing with a hand, the road with rain, a drain, and maybe a river or the sea, with arrows between them.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that litter travels on, past the drain, and does not vanish.
items.art: An empty strip of paper with a small hand drawn at the left end.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: in the Sugar Test, why did the ants stop at the wiped strip?
items.a: The soapy cloth wiped away the smell trail, so the ants could not smell the way. They had to search until they found the smell again.
items.why: A strong answer says the ants follow a smell, and that the wipe took the smell away.

items.p: We should water a potted plant every day, even when the soil is still wet.
items.why: False. If the soil is still wet, more water fills the spaces in the soil and the roots cannot get air. Check with the finger test first.

items.p: A channel or pipe that carries rainwater away from roads is called a ___.
items.why: Drains carry rainwater and used water away. When litter blocks a drain, the water stays on the road.

items.p: A cow is eating vegetable peels and a plastic bag outside a building in Pune.

views.says: The cow is hungry. We should put out more peels for her.
We should keep the bins closed, so the cow does not eat the plastic with the peels.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other one has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that the cow needs food and that plastic hurts her. It might say: keep bins closed, and give peels separately on a leaf, never in a plastic bag.
items.why: Both care about the cow. The plastic is the problem, not the peels.

items.p: This is a potted plant. Write or say the names: leaf, stem, soil, roots, hole at the bottom.
a: hole at the bottom: lets extra water out
items.why: The roots in the soil take in water. The hole at the bottom lets extra water out, so the roots do not sit in water.
items.art: A clay pot cut in half to show the soil and roots inside, with a plant on top and a small hole at the bottom.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to the bin it goes in.
items.why: Food and plant scraps rot, so they are wet waste. Paper, glass, metal and plastic are dry waste, and many of them can be made into new things.
items.art: A green bin and a blue bin, with an idli, a newspaper, an onion skin and a glass bottle around them.

items.p: Why does a crow open her beak and pant on a very hot day?
items.why: Birds cannot sweat like us. Panting moves air over the wet inside of the mouth, which cools the bird down. A shallow plate of water in the shade helps too.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: a wrapper is very small. How can small wrappers block a big drain?
items.a: Many people drop one wrapper each. The rain carries all of them to the same drain. Together they cover the grill.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the rain gathers litter from a whole street into one place.

items.p: Two sisters in Bhubaneswar find ants in the sugar jar.

views.says: Let's spray the ants. They are stealing our sugar.
Let's close the jar tightly and wipe the shelf, so the ants go back outside.

items.ask: Which sister do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer gives a reason from the Sugar Test, for example that wiping takes away the smell trail. It also sees Mitali's point: the family needs their sugar to stay clean.
items.why: Both sisters want the sugar safe. One way hurts the ants. The other way changes what brings them in.

items.p: Draw a bin for a windy balcony that the wind cannot empty. Show how it keeps the litter in.
items.a: For example, a bin with a lid and a stone on top, or a narrow slot to push litter through.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a way to stop the wind lifting light litter, like the fan did in the rain test.
items.art: An empty box shape on a balcony, with wind lines blowing towards it.

items.p: Prerna, a girl in Class 1, tested a paper cup in the bathroom rain test. First the cup floated, then it stopped and stuck to the floor. Why?
opts: The paper soaked up water and got heavy and soft
items.why: Paper soaks up water. Wet paper is heavier and goes soft, so the cup sinks onto the floor. Plastic does not soak up water, so it keeps floating.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? Think about what the rain can carry away.
items.why: The cap, the bag and the wrapper are light and float, so rain can carry them away. A big stone is heavy and stays.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: an old paper cup on the terrace fills with rainwater. Why could this be a problem for people in the house?
items.a: Mosquitoes lay their eggs in small pools of still water. The eggs become mosquitoes, which bite people.
items.why: A strong answer links the litter to the mosquitoes. Litter that holds water gives mosquitoes a place to lay eggs.

items.p: Sort these: which help the plants and animals near us, and which hurt them?
items: a shallow plate of water in the shade
a plastic bag left by the gate
watering a plant when the soil is dry
watering a plant when the soil is already wet
carrying a beetle outside on a card
leaving sugar spilled on the counter
items.why: Helping means looking at what each being really needs. Too much water gives rotten roots, and spilled sugar brings ants indoors.

items.p: If litter washes into a drain, it is gone for ever.
items.why: False. The drain carries the litter on to a canal, a river, a lake or the sea. The litter is still somewhere.

items.p: Draw arrows on this picture to show where the rainwater goes: from the roof, down the road, into the drain and out to the river.
items.why: Rainwater runs downhill from roofs to roads to drains to rivers, and carries litter with it.
items.art: A simple picture of a house with a roof, a road below, a drain at the roadside and a river at the bottom.

items.p: A pot has no hole at the bottom. Why is it hard to water that plant well?
opts: The extra water cannot get out, so the roots sit in water
The plant gets too little water
items.why: Roots need air as well as water. In a pot with no hole, extra water stays in the soil and fills the spaces where air should be.

applications: City workers clear plastic from drains before the monsoon, so that rainwater can flow away.
Many Indian towns ask families to keep wet waste and dry waste in separate bins, so food waste can become compost and dry waste can be recycled.
Saalumarada Thimmakka, a woman from Karnataka, planted banyan trees along a road near her village and watered them for years. They grew into a long, shady avenue.
In 1974, Gaura Devi and the women of Reni village in the Himalayas stood by their trees to stop them being cut. This was part of the Chipko movement.

open_questions.q: Where does all the tiny plastic go when bags and wrappers break into small pieces?
open_questions.why_open: Tiny bits of plastic have been found in rivers, seas, fish and even rain. Scientists are still finding out where they all end up, and what they do to living bodies.

open_questions.q: How do the first ants find the sugar at all?
open_questions.why_open: Scouts wander and smell their way, but how far they can smell food, and how they choose where to search, is still being studied.

open_questions.q: What does a plant feel when the soil goes dry?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure the signals that travel from dry roots to the leaves. What that is like from inside the plant, nobody knows.

maths.problem: In the Bathroom Rain Test, Anjali, a girl in Class 1, tried 5 things. 2 things reached the drain. How many things did not reach the drain?
maths.answer: 3 things did not reach the drain.
maths.explain: There were 5 things. 2 went to the drain. 5 take away 2 is 3. So 3 things stayed or moved only a little.
maths.context: This is about the Bathroom Rain Test, where you poured water near five bits of litter.
maths.why_maths: Taking away the ones that moved tells us how many stayed, so we can see which kind of litter travels.

maths.problem: Arun, the little boy in the story The Red Wrapper, kept a tally with his pocket bin. Monday: 3 wrappers. Tuesday: 1 wrapper. Wednesday: 4 wrappers. On which day did he keep the most? On which day the fewest?
maths.answer: Wednesday had the most, 4. Tuesday had the fewest, 1.
maths.explain: 4 is more than 3, and 3 is more than 1. So Wednesday had the most and Tuesday the fewest. Maybe Wednesday was the day he bought toffees!
maths.context: This is about the pocket bin, where you kept your litter with you for a week.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the days shows when we make the most litter, so we know when to be most careful.

maths.problem: In the Sugar Test, Tanvi, a girl in Class 1, counted ants on the sugar. After 10 minutes there were 2. After 20 minutes there were 6. After 30 minutes there were 12. What is happening to the number of ants? Why might that be?
maths.answer: The number keeps going up: 2, then 6, then 12.
maths.explain: Each count is bigger than the one before. Every ant who finds the sugar adds to the smell trail, so more and more ants find the way.
maths.context: This is about the Sugar Test, where you left sugar out for ants.
maths.why_maths: Seeing the numbers grow helps us spot a pattern, and the pattern tells us something about how the smell trail works.

maths.problem: At the shop, Maya, a girl in Class 1, said no to 2 plastic bags. Her friend said no to 3. How many plastic bags did they not take altogether?
maths.explain: 2 and 3 more make 5. So 5 bags will never end up in a drain or a cow.
maths.context: This is about the trip to the shop with a cloth bag.
maths.why_maths: Adding up shows how small choices by each person add to a bigger difference for the whole family.

founder: ideas/by_topic/caring-for-the-environment.md: the concept activities are about climate zones and the greenhouse effect, which fit higher levels. The SCI Card on Rachel Carson was used for how_we_found_out. Eunice Foote and Svante Arrhenius were not used at this level.
ideas/by_topic/waste.md: the 'Waste is not a waste' week was not used here; it fits the waste units.
Cambridge Stage 2, 1.5 'How can we care for our environment?': litter harms animals and plants; caring for habitats. Its litter-in-soil test is left for Level 2.

Ladder: sci.environment.caring.L3 uses a closed box of moong seedlings and the idea that Earth's water and air go round. This unit does not repeat it, and gives the idea that litter travels with wind and rain.
science: Light, buoyant plastic litter is carried by runoff into storm drains, and blocked drains worsen urban flooding (widely reported for Indian cities during the monsoon).
Plastic bags are found in the rumen of stray cattle in Indian towns, causing impaction (many veterinary case reports from India).
Aedes mosquitoes, which spread dengue, lay eggs in small containers holding rainwater, such as discarded cups, caps and tyres.
Ants lay pheromone trails from food to the nest; wiping a surface, especially with soap, removes the trail and ants lose the path until they find it again.
Plants close their stomata in drying soil, partly through the hormone abscisic acid (ABA) signalled from the roots. Overwatering fills soil pores and starves roots of oxygen.
Birds pant (open-mouth breathing) to lose heat by evaporation.

Roy J. Barker, 'Notes on some ecological effects of DDT sprayed on elms', Journal of Wildlife Management 22 (1958): DDT on fallen elm leaves was taken up by earthworms, and robins that ate the worms died. Rachel Carson, Silent Spring (1962). The US EPA cancelled most uses of DDT in 1972.

Tirukkural 322 (chapter on not killing): sharing your food and caring for many lives is the highest of the precepts. Tattvartha Sutra 5.21: parasparopagraho jivanam, souls render service to one another.

Saalumarada Thimmakka (Karnataka) planted and cared for about 385 banyan trees along roughly 4 km of road between Hulikal and Kudur; Padma Shri, 2019. Gaura Devi led the women of Reni village, Chamoli, in March 1974 (Chipko movement). Sikkim banned plastic bags in 1998.

roots.context: We put clean litter on the bathroom floor and poured a mug of rain. Now we ask what that tells us about the places we share with other beings.

deep_truth.truth: On the bathroom floor, one mug of water carried the toffee wrapper to the drain. The wrapper stuck on the drain's grill, while the pebble beside it stayed put. So light litter dropped on a road travels with the rain, to a drain or a river far away.
deep_truth.habit: We think a wrapper on the ground stays where it fell, and only makes that one spot untidy. But wind and rain move it on, and the harm happens where it ends up, far from the person who dropped it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Bathroom Rain Test, the wrapper and the plastic piece floated to the drain and stuck on the grill, try after try. The pebble stayed in the row. In front of the fan, the light, dry litter blew away too.

three.who_am_i: You are one of many beings who share the same lane, the same drain and the same river. What you drop reaches them.
three.what_is_life: Every living being needs clean water, food and a safe place. Caring for the place near you is caring for the lives there.
three.what_is_this_world: The world around your home is joined by moving water and moving air. They carry things from one place to the next.

roots.thread: Rain falls on every roof and road, and runs into the same drains, lakes and rivers. The same water passes the crow's ledge, the cow's lane and the fish's river. So what one person drops, the water and the wind carry to many others. Keeping one corner clean helps beings we will never meet.

teachings.teaching: Share your food, and care for every living being. Of all the things wise people have taught, this is the greatest.
teachings.link: The Helping Pairs game and the Kind Hands activity ask what each neighbour needs, from a dry plant to a lost beetle. The Kural puts caring for many lives at the top of everything we learn.

teachings.teaching: 'Parasparopagraho jivanam': living beings help one another. Each life is held up by others.
teachings.link: The rain test shows that what we drop reaches others. This Jain teaching says the same about kindness: what we give to one being helps others too.

science.text: Rain and wind move light litter. In Indian cities, plastic and wrappers block drains, and in heavy rain the streets flood.
Plastic breaks into smaller and smaller pieces. Tiny bits have been found in rivers, seas, fish and even rain. What they do to living bodies is still being studied.

other_view.who: Some people who think about why we care for nature
other_view.view: Some people say we should keep our surroundings clean mainly because dirt, floods and mosquitoes harm humans. In this view, caring for crows, cows and ants matters less than caring for people. Others answer that every living being matters for themselves, not only for what they do for us.

practice.title: A gentle hand on a leaf
practice.say: Sit near a plant. Hold one leaf very gently between two fingers, without pulling. Feel how cool and soft it is. Breathe in slowly and out slowly, three times. The plant is feeling your fingers too. Now let the leaf go, just as gently.
practice.kid: Hold one leaf gently. Feel how cool it is. Breathe slowly three times. Let the leaf go gently.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that what we put down in one place can travel to living beings somewhere else? This card tells a true story from about 70 years ago.
how_we_found_out.story: About 70 years ago, towns in the USA sprayed their elm trees with a poison called DDT. The poison was meant to kill the beetles that spread a disease among the elms. People thought the poison would stay on the trees and harm only the beetles. Then, on lawns near the sprayed trees, many robins were found dead or shaking. Robins are birds who eat earthworms. A scientist called Roy Barker looked closely. In autumn, the sprayed leaves fell to the ground. Earthworms ate the fallen leaves, and the poison stayed inside the worms. In spring, the robins ate the worms. So the poison travelled from the tree to the leaf, to the worm, to the bird. In 1962, Rachel Carson, a scientist who studied life in the sea, put many stories like this into a book called Silent Spring. Chemical companies attacked her and said her book was wrong. Other scientists checked, and she was right. In 1972, the USA stopped most uses of DDT.
how_we_found_out.who: Roy Barker, an American scientist who studied insects, and Rachel Carson, an American scientist and writer
how_we_found_out.when: The 1950s (Barker's report came out in 1958), 1962 (Silent Spring) and 1972 (most uses of DDT stopped in the USA)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a poison sprayed on trees stays on the trees and harms only the pests. Barker followed it from the fallen leaves into the earthworms, and then into the robins who ate them.
how_we_found_out.art: An elm tree dropping leaves onto a lawn, an earthworm eating a fallen leaf, and a robin pulling up the worm, with a woman writing at a desk in the corner.
